text: A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of August 31, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 10 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines The Huons Ampule Recall Widens Again — This Time It's the Saline The contamination chain this newsletter has tracked since July (our July 27, August 17, and August 24 issues) has moved past bupivacaine and lidocaine ampules to a new component: sodium chloride flush ampules made by Huons Co. and recalled by Elevaris Medical Devices. In an August 10 letter, Becton Dickinson told customers that certain BD convenience kits and procedure trays may contain the recalled saline, warning that compromised sterility could expose patients to viable microorganisms, endotoxins, or manufacturing debris capable of triggering systemic inflammatory response, infection, microclots, or organ failure. The FDA logged fresh early alerts for Medline and AVID Medical kits on August 24 covering the same underlying saline lot, alongside a Medical Action Industries epidural-kit alert — meaning five separate kit manufacturers are now untangling their supply chains from one contaminated ampule source. As of BD's July 29 count, no serious injuries had been reported from the saline specifically. The practical takeaway hasn't changed from prior issues: check incoming kits and trays against the FDA's lot list by component, not just by kit SKU, since the same manufacturer keeps resurfacing in new products months after the first correction. AHA News · FDA Issues Recall, Alerts for Certain Convenience Kits; Companies Voluntarily Recall Certain IV Fluids · FDA · Early Alert: Convenience Kit Issue from Becton Dickinson A New Union Coalition Sues Over the Same Nursing Loan-Cap Rule a Judge Already Blocked The fight over graduate nursing students' federal loan limits — including CRNA students — isn't over just because a preliminary injunction paused it (our August 3 issue). On August 11, the AFL-CIO, AFSCME, the American Federation of Teachers, and National Nurses United filed a separate suit in U.S. District Court for DC challenging the Department of Education's RISE rule, which would cap graduate nursing borrowing at $20,500 a year and $100,000 aggregate — half the $200,000 aggregate ceiling available to law, medicine, and other programs the rule classifies as "professional." The RISE rule itself narrowed an open-ended "professional degree" test into a closed list of eleven programs, excluding MSN and DNP nursing, along with social work, public health, and several allied-health fields. That case is now consolidated with the earlier litigation on an expedited summary-judgment track, with briefing set to close December 4 — meaning the loan-cap question stays unsettled well into this school year even with the injunction still in place. WSNA · ANA and 9 Nursing Organizations Sue Federal Government Over Loan Limits A New Report Puts This Year's Anesthesiologist Shortfall Near 3,700 Full-Time Positions Medicus Healthcare Solutions' 2026 anesthesia clinician shortage report — a follow-up data point to the workforce trends this newsletter covered August 17 — estimates a current national shortfall of roughly 3,720 full-time-equivalent anesthesiologists, alongside a parallel 3,140 FTE CRNA shortage concentrated in metro markets. The demographic pressure behind the number is stark: 59% of practicing anesthesiologists are 55 or older, 17% are near retirement age, and more than 42% say they plan to leave their current role within two years. On the ground, that's translating into real financial strain for ambulatory surgery centers — the share expecting to pay anesthesia stipends jumped from 28% in 2024 to 44% in 2025, and two-thirds now list anesthesia coverage among their top three financial concerns. For SRNAs finishing clinicals over the next year or two, the market read is unchanged from prior issues: demand is outpacing supply almost everywhere outside the most saturated metros. PR Newswire · Medicus Healthcare Solutions Releases 2026 Edition of Its Report on the Anesthesia Clinician Shortage A New Multidisciplinary Consensus Backs Away From the Blanket SGLT2-Inhibitor Preop Hold Two weeks after this newsletter flagged the tension between SGLT2 inhibitors' renal benefits and their euglycemic-ketoacidosis risk (our August 17 Literature pick), a 2026 multidisciplinary consensus from the Society for Perioperative Assessment and Quality Improvement (SPAQI) has weighed in on the side of nuance rather than a blanket rule. Rather than uniformly stopping SGLT2 inhibitors three to four days before every case, the consensus recommends individualizing the hold based on diabetes status, surgical complexity, expected fasting duration, and comorbid heart failure or chronic kidney disease — weighing the drugs' cardiorenal protection against ketoacidosis risk case by case. It's a meaningful shift from the fixed-interval guidance most programs still have printed on their preop instructions, and it lines up with data cited in APSF's own recent commentary on the topic questioning whether the traditional hold window is longer than the risk actually requires. Registration at asra.com → 📚 From the Literature A 320-Patient Trial Finds Fewer Complications With Opioid-Free Cardiac Anesthesia The OFACAR randomized clinical trial, run at two French tertiary university hospitals, assigned 320 adults undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery to either an opioid-free multimodal regimen (ketamine, dexamethasone, lidocaine, and magnesium sulfate) or a conventional sufentanil-based opioid technique. The primary composite outcome — 30-day neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, or renal complications, or death — occurred in 75.4% of the opioid-free group versus 84.5% of the opioid group (risk ratio 0.90; 95% CI, 0.80–0.99; P = 0.049), driven mainly by fewer cardiovascular and digestive complications; no deaths occurred in the opioid-free arm versus six in the control arm. The authors are notably cautious about their own result: the primary-outcome fragility index means a small number of outcome switches would have erased statistical significance, so they frame OFACAR as hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing until a larger trial confirms it. Worth reading before you assume "opioid-free" automatically means "safer" in cardiac cases — the signal here is real but thin. Guinot, P.-G., et al. (2026). Opioid-free anesthesia in cardiac surgery: The OFACAR randomized clinical trial. Anesthesiology . Virginia came closest to changing that picture: a 2025 bill to eliminate the state's direct-supervision requirement for CRNAs was introduced but didn't reach a floor vote, and sponsors have signaled they intend to reintroduce similar language in the next session rather than let it lapse quietly, the way Rhode Island's H7426 did in June (our August 17 issue). Mississippi and Tennessee show no comparable bill currently active. For SRNAs weighing where to practice after graduation, the reminder is the same one this column keeps making: "opted out federally" and "practices independently" are not the same status, and the gap between them is still wide in more than a dozen states. Confirm against your own pharmacy's supply before assuming availability. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Dexmedetomidine's sedative effect works through the same pathway as natural sleep — which is exactly why it doesn't suppress breathing the way other sedatives do. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α2-adrenergic agonist — roughly eight times more α2-selective than clonidine — that acts primarily at the locus coeruleus in the brainstem. Stimulating α2 receptors there hyperpolarizes noradrenergic neurons, shutting down the tonic norepinephrine output that normally keeps the cortex aroused, which disinhibits the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus and produces a sedative state that resembles natural non-REM sleep far more closely than a GABAergic drug like propofol does. Because the sedation isn't routed through GABA-A receptors, ventilatory drive is largely preserved even at clinically effective doses — the main reason dexmedetomidine has become a favored adjunct for awake fiberoptic intubation and sedation cases where spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes need to stay intact. Board-relevant pearl: know dexmedetomidine's biphasic hemodynamic signature. A loading dose can transiently activate peripheral postsynaptic α2B receptors on vascular smooth muscle, producing brief hypertension with reflex bradycardia, before the drug's dominant central α2A-mediated sympatholysis takes over and produces the more familiar steady-state hypotension and bradycardia. On an exam — or at the bedside — a patient who gets hypertensive right after a dexmedetomidine bolus isn't having a paradoxical reaction; that's the expected peripheral phase, and it's a reason to load slowly (or skip the bolus) in patients who can't tolerate the swing. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 7, 1922 On September 7, 1922, William Stewart Halsted died in Baltimore — remembered today as the father of the American surgical residency system, but also, less famously, one of the founders of regional anesthesia. In 1884, after reading Carl Koller's report that cocaine could numb the eye for ophthalmic surgery, Halsted and several colleagues began injecting cocaine directly into peripheral nerves on themselves and each other, systematically mapping out what became the first true nerve-block techniques — direct ancestors of the brachial plexus and intercostal blocks taught in every regional-anesthesia rotation today. The self-experimentation exacted a brutal personal toll: Halsted developed a lifelong cocaine addiction that nearly derailed his career, and his attempt to treat it left him dependent on morphine for the rest of his life, a struggle he largely concealed while building Johns Hopkins's surgical program into a national model. It's a legacy worth sitting with alongside the technique itself — regional anesthesia's earliest history is inseparable from the people who tested it on their own bodies first, often at real personal cost. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 19-year-old man develops masseter muscle rigidity, tachycardia to the 140s, and rapidly rising end-tidal CO 2 shortly after induction with succinylcholine and sevoflurane for an emergency appendectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention? A Intravenous dantrolene, 2.5 mg/kg, repeated as needed B Intravenous calcium chloride, 10 mg/kg C Switch to a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker and continue the case D Intravenous physostigmine, 1–2 mg Correct answer: A — dantrolene is the only agent that reverses the underlying process in malignant hyperthermia This presentation — masseter rigidity, tachycardia, and a rapidly rising end-tidal CO 2 shortly after exposure to succinylcholine and a volatile agent — is classic for malignant hyperthermia (MH). Dantrolene works by binding the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle, blocking the pathological calcium release that drives the hypermetabolic crisis, and restoring normal excitation-contraction coupling. It's the only pharmacologic agent proven to reverse MH and should be dosed at 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed up to a cumulative 10 mg/kg, alongside stopping all triggering agents and initiating standard MH-crisis supportive care. B is wrong because calcium chloride treats the cardiotoxicity of hyperkalemia — a downstream complication of MH, not the underlying mechanism — and giving calcium can actually worsen the intracellular calcium overload that's driving the crisis. C is wrong because continuing the case ignores the emergency: triggering agents must be stopped immediately and the case aborted, or converted to a non-triggering technique, once the patient is stabilized. D is wrong because physostigmine reverses anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) delirium, a different clinical picture entirely, and has no role in treating MH. A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of August 24, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 9 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines Bupivacaine-Contamination Recall Widens to a Fourth Kit Manufacturer as Medline Issues Correction On August 21, the FDA disclosed a Class I recall — its most serious category — covering Medline convenience kits that pair B. Braun components with Huons Co. bupivacaine hydrochloride in dextrose injection, the same contaminated lot at the center of the B. Braun, Arrow International, and Becton Dickinson corrections this newsletter has tracked since spring (our July 27 and August 17 issues). Medline notified affected customers on June 8 to quarantine the kits and apply over-labels removing the recalled bupivacaine component before continued use; as of a June 19 update, the company had logged no additional serious injuries beyond the 35 B. Braun had already reported. The repeating pattern — one contaminated drug lot rippling through kit after kit for months — is a reminder that "recalled drug, unaffected device" corrections can lag badly at the periphery of a distribution network, and programs should keep checking incoming spinal and epidural trays against the FDA's lot list rather than assuming last month's correction closed the loop. FDA · Convenience Kit Recall: Medline Issues Correction for Kits Containing B. Braun Bupivacaine Components FDA Flags a Class I Recall for Abiomed's 14Fr Introducer Kits Over Clot Risk On August 3, the FDA classified a recall of Abiomed's 14Fr Low Profile Introducer Kits as Class I after the company identified that prolonged indwelling use of the introducer can promote thrombus formation at the insertion site, with the potential for embolization, vessel occlusion, or loss of vascular access during high-acuity cardiac support. The kits are most often placed for Impella heart-pump insertion, putting cardiac anesthesiology and CT surgery teams squarely in the path of the alert; the FDA paired the notice in the same week's bulletin with the already-familiar ResMed Astral ventilator recall (our August 17 issue), a reminder that much of this summer's device-safety attention has centered on prolonged life-support hardware rather than routine OR equipment. Facilities holding affected lots should review Abiomed's field correction for monitoring and exchange guidance before further prolonged placements. Series page at iars.org → 📚 From the Literature A Meta-Analysis Says the 2-Hour Clear-Fluid Fast Doesn't Need to Be 2 Hours in Kids A systematic review and meta-analysis in the British Journal of Anaesthesia examined whether shortening the preoperative clear-fluid fasting window to one hour or less — instead of the traditional two-hour minimum — raises aspiration risk in elective pediatric procedures. Across the pooled cohort, the shorter fast was not associated with any increase in pulmonary aspiration, and it tracked with reduced postoperative nausea, thirst, and hunger scores compared with the traditional window. The authors frame the finding as support for "sip-til-send" protocols already gaining traction in pediatric preop units, and it lines up with the physiology this issue's Knowledge Pearl walks through: clear liquids empty from the stomach fast enough that the extra hour was mostly doing nothing but making kids miserable. Dabke, T., Scott, T. E., & Taylor, B. (2026). Impact of preoperative fasting duration on perioperative complications in elective paediatric procedures: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Anaesthesia, 136 (1), 158–166. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.10.037 ⚖️ Legislation & Scope Tracker DC Regulators Strip "Nurse Anesthesiologist" From Proposed CRNA Title Rules The District of Columbia's Department of Health dropped the term "nurse anesthesiologist" from proposed regulations governing CRNA titling after ASA, the AMA, and the DC Society of Anesthesiologists formally opposed the language, arguing it risked confusing patients about who is administering their anesthesia. ASA publicized the outcome in June as a win in the long-running title fight that also produced AANA's decision to withdraw its federal trademark applications for the same phrase after a roughly two-year opposition proceeding (our July 13 issue) — two separate venues, same underlying dispute, both resolved against the "nurse anesthesiologist" label for now. ASA · ASA Applauds DC Department of Health's Rejection of "Misleading" Nurse Anesthesiologist Phrase Ohio's New "Collaboration" Law Complicates the State's Own Federal Opt-Out When Ohio notified CMS it no longer needed the federal physician-supervision rule for CRNAs (our July 20 issue), it looked like straightforward momentum toward independent CRNA practice. House Bill 52 — signed by Governor Mike DeWine on March 10 and in effect since June 8 — tells a more complicated story: it replaces the old physician-supervision requirement with a "collaboration" model, but the fine print still requires a collaborating physician, dentist, or podiatrist to be physically present in the facility for the induction, maintenance, and emergence of general anesthesia, and adds a new mandatory disclosure telling patients by name who is administering their anesthesia. Unsurprisingly, ASA and AANA have described the same law in opposite terms — ASA calling it a preservation of "physician-led anesthesia care," AANA calling it a "modernized" CRNA practice law — a reminder that scope-of-practice fights increasingly turn on how supervision gets defined on paper, not simply whether it's required at all. Confirm against your own pharmacy's supply before assuming availability. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Clear liquids don't sit in the stomach the way solids do — that's the whole basis for "sip-til-send." Clear, non-particulate liquids (water, pulp-free juice, black coffee, sports drinks) empty from the stomach largely by first-order kinetics driven by volume and hydrostatic pressure, with a half-emptying time typically under 15 minutes regardless of whether the starting volume was 150 mL or 450 mL — residual volume converges back toward a low fasting baseline well within an hour for most patients. That's mechanistically different from solids, fats, and protein-containing liquids like milk, which trigger antral grinding, pyloric sieving, and duodenal feedback inhibition that can stretch gastric emptying out past four to six hours. ASA and European (ESAIC) guidance has permitted clear liquids up to two hours before elective anesthesia for years; the data in this issue's Literature pick is pushing programs to ask whether even that two-hour buffer is doing much beyond making patients thirstier — particularly in pediatrics, where dehydration and hypoglycemia from prolonged fasting are a bigger day-to-day problem than a hypothetical aspiration the volume-and-timing data doesn't support. Board-relevant distinction: know the classic 2-4-6-8 fasting rule (clears–breast milk–infant formula/light meal–solids/full meal), but also know why clear liquids get the shortest window — NPO status is fundamentally a volume-and-acidity risk model, and clear liquids fail to accumulate stomach volume the way solids do. On an exam, don't conflate "recent PO intake" (a genuine aspiration risk factor regardless of what any guideline says) with "guideline non-compliance" (missed the stated fasting window) — the former calls for a full-stomach precaution; the latter, in an otherwise low-risk elective case, often doesn't. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 29, 1809 On August 29, 1809, Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts — the physician, essayist, and Harvard anatomy professor who, in a November 21, 1846 letter to William T. G. Morton, proposed naming the new phenomenon "anaesthesia," from the Greek for "without sensation," and further suggested "anaesthetic" for the agent and "to anaesthetize" for the act of administering it. Morton had given his first public ether demonstration barely five weeks earlier, on October 16, 1846, in the same city Holmes called home — the operating theater now preserved as the Ether Dome at Massachusetts General Hospital, walking distance from where this year's AANA Congress crowds gathered this week (see Headlines, above). Holmes's proposed vocabulary stuck almost immediately and has outlived nearly everything else written about ether in 1846. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 68-year-old man undergoing an interscalene brachial plexus block with 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine becomes acutely agitated, then develops perioral numbness and tinnitus, followed roughly 90 seconds later by a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Shortly afterward, the monitor shows a wide-complex tachycardia. In addition to airway management and benzodiazepines for seizure control, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment? A Intravenous lidocaine to suppress the ventricular arrhythmia B 20% lipid emulsion, administered as an intravenous bolus followed by a continuous infusion C Standard ACLS cardiac-arrest dosing of epinephrine, 1 mg IV push D Intravenous calcium chloride to stabilize the cardiac membrane Correct answer: B — 20% lipid emulsion is first-line treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity The sequence — agitation and perioral numbness, then tinnitus, then seizure, then cardiovascular collapse — is the textbook progression of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) following inadvertent intravascular uptake of a large-volume amide block. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, 20% lipid emulsion should be given promptly alongside airway management and seizure control: a bolus (roughly 1.5 mL/kg lean body mass over about a minute), repeated once or twice for persistent cardiovascular instability, followed by a continuous infusion. The mechanism is thought to involve both a "lipid sink" that pulls lipophilic local anesthetic out of cardiac tissue and improved delivery of fatty acids to stressed myocardial mitochondria. A is wrong because lidocaine is itself an amide local anesthetic that competes at the same sodium channels and can worsen LAST rather than treat it. C is wrong because ASRA guidance specifically recommends reducing standard ACLS epinephrine doses (to roughly 1 mcg/kg or less) in LAST, since full-dose epinephrine can impair resuscitation with lipid emulsion and provoke more malignant arrhythmias in a heart already destabilized by sodium-channel blockade. D treats hyperkalemia or calcium-channel-blocker toxicity, not LAST, and has no established role here. SGLT2 inhibitors — empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, and others — block glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, producing glycosuria, mild volume contraction, and a metabolic shift toward fat oxidation and ketogenesis, the same mechanism behind their renal- and cardio-protective effects (see this week's Literature pick). Under the physiologic stress of surgery — fasting, insulin withdrawal, catecholamine surge — that shift can tip into ketoacidosis, but because the drug's glycosuric effect keeps blood glucose from climbing, patients can present with a significant anion-gap ketoacidosis while their glucose reads a deceptively normal 130–180 mg/dL. Providers trained to equate DKA with a glucose in the 400s can miss it entirely. Etomidate potentiates GABA-A receptor chloride currents like other induction agents, producing rapid hypnosis with minimal effect on myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, or heart rate - the reason it remains a go-to induction agent for hemodynamically unstable, cardiac, and trauma patients even as broader anesthetic choices narrow this year (see this week's Drug Shortage Watch). That same stability comes with a well-known cost: etomidate reversibly inhibits 11β-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in the adrenal cortex, suppressing endogenous cortisol synthesis for roughly 6–8 hours after even a single induction dose. The suppression is usually clinically silent after a single bolus in an otherwise healthy patient, but it's why etomidate infusions fell out of favor for ICU sedation and why critically ill or septic patients who receive even one induction dose are sometimes considered for stress-dose steroid coverage. Etomidate's other signature quirks - myoclonus on induction (not seizure activity, though it can look like one), a comparatively high incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting, and pain on injection - are all worth anticipating regardless of the adrenal question. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 10, 1898 In Greifswald, Germany, surgeon August Bier administered what is generally credited as the first spinal anesthetic given specifically to enable surgery: a solution of cocaine injected into the subarachnoid space of his assistant, August Hildebrandt, after an earlier attempt on a patient had failed when too much of the drug leaked from a loose-fitting syringe. Bier and Hildebrandt then tested the block on each other - reportedly checking pain tolerance with pinpricks, cigar burns, and blows to the shin - in a demonstration that reads more like a dare than a clinical trial by modern standards. Both men suffered severe post-dural-puncture headaches for days afterward, an early and unintentional demonstration of the complication that would occupy anesthesia researchers for the next century. MH is caused by a defect, most commonly in the RYR1 gene, that leaves the ryanodine receptor abnormally sensitive to triggering agents (all volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine), producing uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and a hypermetabolic cascade. Dantrolene works directly at that defect, inhibiting calcium release through RYR1, and should be pushed immediately at 2.5 mg/kg, repeated up to 10 mg/kg or more until signs resolve - alongside discontinuing all triggering agents, hyperventilating with 100% oxygen at high flow, and starting active cooling. C treats a downstream consequence - hyperkalemia - rather than the underlying calcium dysregulation, and isn't first-line; standard hyperkalemia measures are adjuncts once dantrolene is underway, not substitutes for it. D does nothing to interrupt the hypermetabolic process driving the tachycardia and would delay definitive treatment. This week's FDA alert on sevoflurane is a sharp reminder that volatile anesthetics aren't metabolically inert. Mitochondria generate the ATP that excitable, oxygen-hungry tissue — brain and heart chief among it — depends on minute to minute, and volatile agents are known to mildly suppress mitochondrial electron transport chain activity as part of how they produce anesthesia. In a patient with a normal mitochondrial reserve, that suppression is trivial and fully reversible. In a patient carrying a pathogenic mitochondrial variant — like the MT-ND4 m.11232T>C mutation implicated in the current cases — baseline oxidative capacity is already reduced, and volatile-agent suppression on top of that can tip vulnerable tissue into energy failure, producing exactly the picture being reported: unexplained neurologic devastation or cardiac collapse in patients with no other risk factors. The practical takeaway for boards and bedside alike isn't "avoid volatiles in everyone" — it's recognizing when mitochondrial disease is on the differential (unexplained lactic acidosis, myopathy, prior anesthetic complications, suggestive family or ancestry history) and defaulting toward total intravenous or regional techniques in those patients, since propofol and regional anesthesia don't carry the same electron-transport-chain liability at clinical doses. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 25, 1894 Harold Griffith was born in Montreal on this date — the anesthetist who, on January 23, 1942, gave the world its first practical neuromuscular blocking agent. Working with resident Enid Johnson at the Homeopathic Hospital of Montreal, Griffith injected an extract of curare, Intocostrin , into a 20-year-old undergoing an appendectomy, producing profound muscle relaxation without deepening the ether anesthesia already in progress. Before that afternoon, adequate relaxation for abdominal surgery meant anesthetizing patients dangerously deep; Griffith's report, published later that year, opened the door to lighter, safer anesthesia paired with deliberate paralysis — the conceptual split between hypnosis, analgesia, and relaxation that still organizes how anesthesia is taught today. A qualitative peripheral nerve stimulator shows a train-of-four with no fade appreciable to the observer. Which statement best describes this scenario? A Residual neuromuscular blockade has been definitively ruled out because the train-of-four shows no fade B Clinically significant residual blockade can still be present; qualitative train-of-four monitoring reliably detects fade only once the train-of-four ratio has fallen below about 0.4, well short of the 0.9 threshold associated with these symptoms C These findings are more consistent with emergence delirium than with neuromuscular blockade D A normal train-of-four by any method excludes residual paralysis as a cause of postoperative airway obstruction Correct answer: B — Qualitative TOF can look reassuring while real residual blockade persists The vignette describes classic signs of residual neuromuscular blockade: upper-airway obstruction, uncoordinated movement, and inability to sustain a head lift — a bedside surrogate for a train-of-four ratio below roughly 0.9, the threshold below which pharyngeal function and airway protection are impaired. The trap in this question is the "normal" qualitative TOF: the human eye reliably detects fade only when the train-of-four ratio has already dropped well below 0.4, so a qualitative twitch monitor can look unremarkable at ratios between roughly 0.4 and 0.9 — precisely the range where clinically meaningful residual paralysis lives. This gap is the rationale behind APSF's ongoing push for quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (which reports an actual numeric TOF ratio) as the more reliable standard before extubation. Emergence delirium doesn't produce upper-airway obstruction or an inability to sustain a head lift as its primary features, so C is a weaker fit for this clinical picture. D repeats the same qualitative-versus-quantitative trap as A — a "normal" TOF by qualitative assessment never fully excludes clinically important residual blockade, whereas a quantitative TOF ratio at or above 0.9 does. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients (most often via RYR1 mutations), causing the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to dump calcium into the muscle cytoplasm uncontrollably. That flood of calcium drives sustained contraction, runaway heat production, and skyrocketing oxygen consumption — the hypermetabolic state that produces the classic triad of rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, and fever. Dantrolene binds the RYR1 receptor directly and blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cutting off the process at its source rather than just treating the downstream fever or acidosis. Initial dosing is 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated every 5–10 minutes until symptoms resolve — there is no fixed maximum in an ongoing crisis. Because a single reaction doesn't fully rule a patient out or in, current guidance leans on a short screening history (personal or family MH reaction, and any prior genetic testing) to decide who actually needs formal RYR1 / CACNA1S / STAC3 sequencing, rather than testing everyone with a vague family rumor of "anesthesia problems." 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History June 17, 1931 On June 17, 1931, Agatha Hodgins founded the National Association of Nurse Anesthetists — the organization that would become today's AANA — in Cleveland, Ohio. C describes neuraxial (spinal/epidural) sympathetic blockade, not a peripheral fascial plane block. D is incorrect — the phrenic nerve runs nowhere near the TAP plane; diaphragmatic irritation from pneumoperitoneum isn't addressed by this block. Unlike neostigmine, which reverses neuromuscular blockade indirectly by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and raising synaptic acetylcholine, sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that forms a tight 1:1 host-guest complex directly around the steroidal neuromuscular blocker molecule in the plasma. This encapsulation creates a concentration gradient that pulls free rocuronium or vecuronium off nicotinic receptors and out of the neuromuscular junction, back into plasma for renal clearance as an inactive complex. The practical payoff: sugammadex can reverse even profound (deep) blockade reliably, works faster than neostigmine at comparable depths, and — because it doesn't act on acetylcholinesterase — carries none of neostigmine's muscarinic side effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions), so it doesn't require co-administration with an antimuscarinic like glycopyrrolate. It has no reversal activity against benzylisoquinolinium blockers (e.g., cisatracurium) or succinylcholine, since those aren't steroidal molecules it can encapsulate. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 1940 In July 1940, the American Society of Anesthesiologists published the first issue of Anesthesiology , under founding editor-in-chief Henry S.
